name: Orbitz
tierWhy: Clearly Canadian stopped making Orbitz by 1999 and said in 2015 that it no longer had the equipment to make it. Old bottles sell to collectors; we found no official revival.[^5]

title: Orbitz (1996–1999): the drink with floating gel balls · Spectre Brands
description: Orbitz was a fruit drink with floating gel balls from Clearly Canadian. It was a hit in 1997, its sales fell almost 85% in early 1998 and it was gone by 1999.

card.blurb: Clearly Canadian’s 1996 drink with colored gel balls suspended in fruit-flavored water. It was a sensation with teenagers for a year; first-half sales fell from $9.4M in 1997 to $1.46M in 1998, and the company stopped making it.

hero.standfirst: A drink you could chew. Teenagers tried it once.
hero.deck: Orbitz was a [non-carbonated fruit drink](/category/consumer/) from Clearly Canadian, the Vancouver maker of flavored sparkling waters, and it had been discontinued by 1999. Its selling point was the small balls of gellan gum that hung, without sinking, in the liquid. Launched in 1996 for 12- to 17-year-olds, it sold a million cases in its first months, by the company’s account, and was a hit in 1997. In the first half of 1998 its sales fell by almost 85%. The company said this was the life cycle it had expected; by 1999 the drink was gone. This page is built from [contemporary press and Clearly Canadian’s own SEC filings](/about/#sources).

findings.title: Built to be talked about, not repeated.
findings.text: Its spokesman said the aim was to make whoever brought Orbitz into a room “the center of attention for a few moments.”[^1] Reviewers called it a lava lamp, tapioca and worse.[^1][^2]

findings.title: The collapse was in the plan.
findings.text: When first-half sales fell from $9.4M to $1.46M, the marketing chief said: “Our expected life-cycle of the product is coming true.”[^4]

findings.title: No advertising budget to rescue it.
findings.text: Clearly Canadian relied on product placement, sampling and events, saying advertising was “too mass for our products and, quite frankly, not affordable.”[^4]

findings.title: The parent kept shrinking.
findings.text: Clearly Canadian’s revenue fell from $34.9M in 1998 to $20.5M in 2002, with losses in every year after 1998. Its own filings warned that beverage brands may last “a few years” before tastes change.[^6]
